Some lands are known for their beauty, others for their history. But Palestine carries a story that stretches far beyond its borders, a story written in ancient streets, olive trees and generations of people who call it home. This is Palestine! Welcome to Palestine! 🇵🇸❤️ Located in the Middle East, Palestine consists of two territories: the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, along the eastern Mediterranean. In Bethlehem, the birthplace of Jesus, the ancient Church of the Nativity stands as one of Christianity's most important historic sites. Then there's Jericho, one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, where thousands of years of human history can still be felt. In Nablus, traditional markets, historic architecture and the famous Palestinian knafeh reveal a culture rich in flavour and tradition. And in Battir, ancient stone terraces, olive groves and beautiful landscapes tell the story of generations connected to the land. But Palestine is more than ancient buildings and beautiful scenery. It is a place of deep cultural traditions, distinctive embroidery, traditional music, delicious food and remarkable hospitality. From its historic cities to its Mediterranean coastline, Palestine carries a heritage that deserves to be discovered and remembered. So, if you could experience one place in Palestine, where would you go? Saudi Arabia's crown prince publicly demands a Palestinian state. Yet his fund is paying Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who has said recognizing a Palestinian state would reward terror. The crown prince is Mohammed bin Salman. The fund he chairs committed $2 billion to Kushner's brand new firm, and Kushner now negotiates Gaza's future with a plan that would turn Gaza's coast into tourism and towers. But in private, The Atlantic reported, the crown prince told Biden's secretary of state, "Do I care personally about the Palestinian issue? I don't, but my people do, so I need to make sure this is meaningful." A Saudi official called that account incorrect. Six months after Kushner left Trump's first White House, the crown prince's fund made that $2 billion commitment to Kushner's firm, Affinity Partners, though Kushner had no track record running an investment fund. Since then, the fund has paid Kushner's firm an estimated $110 million in fees, Democrats in Congress say. The Wall Street Journal reported that Kushner's firm would invest Saudi money in Israel, and that the crown prince would have to personally approve those investments. Kushner's firm became the biggest shareholder of Israel's largest insurer, and Israel's leading business paper called it a "Saudi fund." The Kushner family and Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, have been close for decades. When Netanyahu stayed at their New Jersey home, Jared gave up his bed and slept in the basement. Four months into the war in Gaza, Kushner told an audience at Harvard, "I think proactively recognizing a Palestinian state would essentially be rewarding an act of terror." Among the men Trump has negotiating Gaza's future is his own son-in-law: Netanyahu's close family friend, whose brand new firm the crown prince's fund backed with $2 billion. In October 2009, American actress and UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador Mia Farrow visited the Gaza Strip, where Palestinian families were still struggling to recover from Israel’s military offensive known as Operation Cast Lead. The assault, which lasted from December 27, 2008, to January 18, 2009, killed over 1400 Palestinians, including hundreds of children. Thousands of homes were destroyed or damaged, along with schools, hospitals, and essential infrastructure. By the time Farrow arrived, nine months had passed since the offensive began, yet families were still living among the destruction, with reconstruction severely restricted by Israel’s blockade of Gaza. #Gaza #OperationCastLead ##MiaFarrow #UNICEF  During her visit, Farrow met Palestinian children and families in Beit Lahiya and visited al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, witnessing the humanitarian consequences of the war and the ongoing restrictions on everyday life. Gaza had already been subjected to years of increasingly severe movement and trade restrictions, particularly since 2007, leaving its population struggling with shortages of building materials, medical supplies, and other necessities. This footage is from 2009, long before the devastation that began in October 2023. It is an important reminder that the suffering of Palestinian children in Gaza did not begin in 2023, and neither did the international warnings about their conditions.
